Chapter 2: Finding a Place in the World of Theater
If you've ever felt like you just didn't fit in, theater can feel like a sanctuary. Think about those moments backstage or in echoing rehearsal halls—where all the usual rules just... don't matter. Here, being loud or quirky, even a little over-the-top, isn't just accepted—it's celebrated. My first taste of this freedom? It came in high school. The drama club quickly became my second home.
Auditions were always nerve-wracking—my heart would pound, palms sweaty—but the rush you get when you land a part? Nothing compares. And then there’s the bond with the cast, the excited buzz before opening night, and that feeling of working together toward something bigger than yourself. For the first time, being different actually felt like a gift.
Then came college, and suddenly the world of theater got a whole lot wider. The university stage was bigger, the competition stiffer, and the people? So talented—and from every walk of life. It was easy to feel a little out of your depth, maybe even a bit intimidated by the confidence and skill of others. But slowly, a new thought crept in: Maybe there’s a place for me here too. Rehearsing lines, building sets, and collaborating on productions taught me discipline and commitment—skills that stuck long after the curtain fell.
But, even in this creative space, those old insecurities would sometimes sneak in. There was pressure to stand out, to succeed, to prove you belonged. I remember nights wondering: Is this dream even realistic? Is my talent enough? Are the sacrifices worth it? The fear of failing was always there, but so was the urge to keep going.
Outside the theater, the struggle with identity never really stopped. The world was changing, but not quite fast enough. Being openly gay still felt risky, especially in a field where how you’re seen can mean everything. There was this constant balancing act—wanting to be yourself, but worried about what might happen if you were. Friendships grew deeper through shared vulnerability, but the most personal truths? Those often stayed hidden.
What really helped were the mentors and role models I met along the way. Directors, teachers, older performers—they offered guidance and encouragement when I needed it most. Their belief in me was a lifeline during rough patches. Watching them live authentically, take risks, and embrace imperfection showed me that success is rarely a straight line. It’s full of detours, and sometimes, yes, even failures.
One of the biggest lessons I learned was the value of perseverance. Rejection is just part of the deal—missed auditions, harsh critiques, and lost opportunities. But each setback is a chance to learn, grow, and try again. Over time, I realized that resilience matters more than raw talent. What really counts is showing up, again and again, even after disappointment.
Theater also gave me a safe place to experiment with who I was. Getting to step into different roles, try on new personas, and explore unfamiliar emotions—it was like testing out different versions of myself. Sometimes, the lines between character and reality felt blurry. But that made it easier to imagine a life where being authentic was actually possible.
Looking back, those years in the theater were about so much more than putting on a show. They were about finding a place to belong, learning to trust others, and slowly starting to accept myself. The stage offered a glimpse of how life might look if difference was something to be embraced—not hidden away. That lesson took years to sink in, but the seeds were planted right there—in the glow of the footlights and the laughter of castmates.
